title: How to Use a Wooden Spurtle for Sourdough English Muffins
meta_description: Master the art of sourdough English muffins with the perfect tool. Learn how to use a wooden spurtle to mix, fold, and scrape your sourdough dough.
html:
There is something uniquely satisfying about a warm, nooks-and-crannies-filled English muffin toasted with a slab of salted butter. But if you’ve tried making them at home, you know that sourdough english muffin dough can be a bit temperamental. It’s stickier than a standard loaf and requires a delicate touch to keep those air pockets intact.

While many bakers rely on heavy mixers or bulky spatulas, the secret to a smooth workflow is often a simpler tool. Enter the wooden spurtle. If you haven't used one, think of it as the Swiss Army knife of the sourdough world—part stirring stick, part spatula, and entirely essential for managing sticky doughs.

Why a Spurtle is Ideal for Sourdough English Muffin Dough

Sourdough English muffins require a high hydration level to achieve that signature open crumb. When you first mix your flour, water, and active starter, the mixture is a shaggy, sticky mess. A standard spoon often leaves clumps of dry flour at the bottom of the bowl, and a large whisk can be overkill for small batches.

The Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set (2 PCS) solves this problem. The skinny spurtle spatula is designed to reach into the tight corners of a mixing bowl or a starter jar, ensuring every bit of flour is incorporated. Because it's narrow, it cuts through the dough without deflating the gases produced by your wild yeast, which is crucial for the rise of your muffins.

Step-by-Step: Mixing Your Sourdough Dough with a Spurtle

To get the most out of your tools, follow this sequence when prepping your batch. Using the right tool at the right stage prevents you from overworking the dough.

  1. The Initial Mix: Start by combining your active sourdough starter and warm water. Use the Danish-style dough stick from the set to whisk these together quickly. The loop design of the dough whisk breaks up starter clumps efficiently.
  2. Incorporating Flour: Gently fold in your flour and salt. This is where the skinny wooden spurtle shines. Use a stirring motion to bring the flour from the edges into the center.
  3. The Shaggy Stage: Once the dough comes together into a shaggy mass, use the spurtle to press the dough against the side of the bowl. This helps develop the gluten without the mess of kneading by hand.
  4. Jar Scraping: If you are mixing your starter in a separate jar, the slim profile of the spurtle allows you to scrape the sides clean, ensuring no wasted starter remains stuck to the glass.

Managing Sticky Sourdough English Muffin Dough

One of the biggest frustrations with sourdough English muffin dough is how it clings to everything. If you use a wide silicone spatula, you often end up with a thick layer of dough stuck to the tool, which means less dough in your pan.

The smooth, non-porous finish of the Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set (2 PCS) allows the dough to slide off more easily. When it's time to divide the dough into individual muffins, use the spurtle to gently nudge the dough into your rings or onto the griddle. Its thin edge acts like a precision tool, allowing you to shape the muffins without degassing them.

Maintaining Your Wooden Baking Tools

To keep your wooden tools in top shape, avoid the dishwasher. The high heat and harsh detergents can cause the wood to crack or warp over time. Instead, a quick rinse with warm, soapy water and a towel dry is all you need.

For those who bake frequently, I recommend rubbing a small amount of food-grade mineral oil into the wood every few months. This creates a moisture barrier that prevents the dough from sticking and keeps the wood from drying out, ensuring your spurtle remains a staple in your kitchen for years.

Beyond the Muffin: Multi-Purpose Uses

While we've focused on English muffins, these tools are incredibly versatile. The Danish dough whisk is perfect for heavy rye breads or cinnamon roll dough, while the skinny spurtle is the gold standard for feeding your sourdough starter. Because they are non-scratch, you can use them in expensive ceramic bowls or non-stick pans without worrying about damage.

Whether you're stirring a thick porridge, mixing a small batch of batter, or maintaining your starter culture, having a dedicated set of wooden stirrers simplifies the process and keeps your counters cleaner.

FAQ

Can I use a spurtle instead of a dough whisk?

Yes, but they serve different purposes. The dough whisk is better for the very first stage of mixing liquid and flour to avoid lumps. The spurtle is superior for folding, scraping the bowl, and handling the dough once it has thickened.

Why is a wooden tool better than plastic for sourdough?

Wood is naturally more durable and doesn't flex under the weight of heavy doughs. Additionally, high-quality wooden tools don't leach chemicals into your food and are generally more sustainable than plastic alternatives.

How do I stop the sourdough English muffin dough from sticking to the tool?

Lightly dip your spurtle in water or a tiny bit of olive oil before stirring. This creates a thin barrier that prevents the sticky dough from adhering to the wood.
